    Instructor Notes

    Status and intended audience

    This is an initial teaching scaffold for a two-day course. Topics 1 and 3 are existing contributions; Topics 2 and 4 extend them with prepared examples. Timings are estimates to revise after a novice walkthrough and pilot delivery. The intended learner has domain knowledge but little formal programming training.

    The outcome is to specify, explain, investigate, and assess small AI-generated programs. Learners are not expected to independently write a web back end, design class hierarchies, implement authentication, or deploy a production service.

    Suggested two-day schedule

    Time Day 1 Day 2
    09:00–09:20 Welcome, expectations, readiness check Recap: inputs, behaviour, evidence
    09:20–10:20 Topic 1: first half Topic 3: first half
    10:20–10:35 Break Break
    10:35–11:35 Topic 1: second half Topic 3: second half
    11:35–12:00 Guided practice and questions Guided practice and questions
    12:00–12:45 Lunch Lunch
    12:45–14:00 Topic 2: orientation and tracing Topic 4: parts and requests
    14:00–14:15 Break Break
    14:15–15:30 Topic 2: reuse, settings, investigation Topic 4: storage, access, specification
    15:30–15:50 Repair clinic or unfinished practice Architecture/specification clinic
    15:50–16:00 Reflection and feedback Reflection and feedback

    Each new topic has 65 minutes of explanation/demonstration and 85 minutes of exercises, including discussion and feedback. Practice periods are additional support, not hidden requirements for core exercises. Topic 2’s exit ticket is within its 150 minutes; final reflection reviews the broader course.

    Preparation

    1. Follow learner setup from a fresh extracted ZIP on the operating systems used in the workshop. Check Python 3.9+, SQLite, browser module loading, and browser storage. No packages need installing.
    2. Start python3 episodes/files/serve.py (Windows: replace python3 with py -3). Keep it running for both examples. Check URLs, developer tools, and zoom.
    3. Use a fresh database or rename the previous one while the server is stopped. Default: episodes/files/activities.sqlite3. Reset task lists with each version’s Clear practice tasks button. Starter and solution store separately.
    4. Complete both lessons’ exercises yourself. Arrange a second browser/profile on the same laptop. Check restart persistence using the same database.
    5. Provide the ZIP, worksheet, and request transcripts before class. Print or download evidence for restricted devices or connectivity failures.
    6. Communicate AI account arrangements and the route without an account. Test any live generation beforehand.
    7. Organise helpers and shared notes. Invite learners to signal when they need help without requiring a public explanation.

    Teaching approach

    Introduce one small idea, model reading it, ask for a prediction, then run or inspect it together. Allow quiet thinking before pair discussion. Offer individual participation and rotate optional driver/navigator roles. Assess explanations and evidence rather than speed or exact syntax. Expand terms on first use and name the destination before switching windows.

    The prepared starter rejects empty descriptions but accepts spaces. Let learners predict and observe before revealing .trim(). The solution changes the validator only. Comparing a newly AI-generated version belongs in the clinic, after the common objectives are met.

    In Topic 4 move between browser action, selected request, response, and visible result. Keep serve.py implementation details in instructor discussion unless asked. The goal is reasoning across boundaries.

    Formative checks

    Check Evidence of intended understanding
    Locate validation Identifies validateTask, not CSS or storage code.
    Trace spaces Length is 3; starter returns true despite requirement.
    Return versus display Return reaches caller; textContent changes display.
    Recognise import storage.js is local; JSON is built in; no JS packages installed.
    Recognise class Distinguishes Task, reading, property, method.
    Inspect GET/POST Identifies method, path, payload, status, response.
    Invalid activity Spaces pass browser required check; server returns 400; no insertion.
    Persistence Tasks follow browser/profile and origin; activities follow server/database.
    Save versus display A GET can contain a record omitted by faulty rendering.
    Access scenario Requires server permission check; hiding a button is insufficient.

    Use the Topic 2 transfer question and Topic 4 specification as individual assessment before discussion. Invite one concept that now makes sense and one remaining question during reflection. Adjust explanations from those responses.

    Fallback delivery

    Constraint Equivalent participation
    No AI account/service Describe intended change, then inspect prepared repair and repeat checks.
    Python cannot run Pair with working laptop or predict before projected demonstration.
    Developer tools inaccessible Annotate supplied request transcripts.
    Only one browser/profile Predict separate-browser results and compare prepared observations.
    Storage restricted Use permitted fresh profile or prepared observations.
    Time pressure Preserve prediction, repair, one request inspection, persistence reasoning, final specification.

    Class design, package installation, full login flows, SQL, and public deployment are extensions. Class recognition remains a short core activity.

    Example design and boundaries

    The task manager is browser-side code with a local storage helper module. The server delivers assets but does not save tasks. Both versions support adding, completing/reopening, deleting, refreshing, and clearing practice data.

    The activity tracker uses Python’s standard HTTP and SQLite libraries, serves an explicit set of lesson assets, exposes GET/POST /api/activities, validates on the server, and persists accepted records. New records have a server-assigned ID and completed: false. The server binds only to loopback.

    ACTIVITY_DB selects a database file for separate sessions. On macOS/Linux:

    BASH 

    ACTIVITY_DB=/tmp/afternoon-activities.sqlite3 python3 episodes/files/serve.py --port 8001

    In PowerShell, set it before starting:

    POWERSHELL 

    $env:ACTIVITY_DB = "$env:TEMP/afternoon-activities.sqlite3"
py -3 episodes/files/serve.py --port 8001

    Use a new filename for fresh seed data. The parent directory must exist. Port changes also change the browser storage origin.

    This is a local teaching server, not a production deployment template. It has no login, roles, update/delete API, or concurrency-conflict exercise. Role and hosting scenarios are proposed requirements. The stale-display case is prepared evidence, not an intentional bug in the runnable activity tracker.

    Author checks and maintenance

    From the repository root, rebuild the archive after changing examples or data:

    BASH 

    python3 scripts/package-examples.py
python3 scripts/check-examples.py

    The check script uses temporary storage and an ephemeral loopback port; it does not change practice records. A browser walkthrough is also needed to assess interaction, accessibility, and teaching flow. With sandpaper installed, run:

    R 

    sandpaper::validate_lesson()
sandpaper::build_lesson()

    Inspect episode order, downloads, figure descriptions, challenge/solution nesting, learner/instructor views, and relative links in the rendered site. Do not edit generated files under site/.

    References: Workbench episode structure, memory and cognitive load, and building skill with feedback.

    From Ideas to Computational Problems

    Instructor Notes

    Teaching approach: Build the task-manager workflow live with learners. Ask for predictions and learner suggestions before showing solutions. Keep explanations short and alternate them with exercises.

    Common misconceptions:

    • “AI will figure out what I mean.” Ask which assumptions the agent made.
    • “Pseudocode must look like real code.” Emphasize clarity rather than syntax.
    • “Every step must be a function.” Prefer functions with meaningful responsibilities.
    • “State means a database.” Contrast in-memory state with persistent storage.
    • “If the AI produces an app, the task is complete.” Require behavioural tests.

    Formative checkpoints:

    • Can another person follow the workflow without guessing?
    • What happens with missing or invalid input?
    • What repeats when there are 100 items instead of three?
    • Which operations depend on earlier results?
    • What example would prove that the feature works?

    Exit ticket: Describe the inputs, outputs, state, decisions, repetition, and main steps of a meal recommender that uses ingredients already available at home.


    Understanding What AI Is Building

    Delivery notes

    Use the four timing blocks above; challenge times include discussion and feedback. Keep each explanation short and let learners predict before running code. Give quiet thinking time before pair comparison; learners can also work alone. The reading snippets are selected portions, not instructions to type a whole app.

    Before class, test the starter and solution through the supplied server. Both normal and private-browser storage must be checked for the browsers you teach. If storage is disabled or contains malformed data, use a fresh browser profile or the prepared observation evidence rather than spending the lesson on repair.

    Misconceptions to revisit: defining a function calls it; returning displays; an import always means installing a package; an object requires a custom class; no exception means correct output; an AI explanation proves a change works.

    The classes example is recognition only. Package-management commands and class design are optional extensions. The core repair can be completed without an AI account by revealing the solution after a learner has explained the intended change. See the shared instructor notes.


    Data, Files and Structured Information

    Instructor notes

    Preparation: Have data/activities.csv, an empty output/ folder, and a text editor ready. Test the conversion exercise with the intended AI coding agent beforehand.

    Live demonstration: Compare CSV and JSON representations of the same records. Ask learners to predict which values change type. Show a missing-path error and a CSV field containing commas.

    Common misconceptions: A file extension guarantees its format; CSV preserves numeric types; missing means zero; IDs must always be numbers; a script finishing without errors proves its output is correct.

    Formative checks: Ask learners to identify relative paths, explain CSV quoting, distinguish JSON strings from Booleans, and describe how to preserve leading zeros.

    Timing: 85 minutes teaching and 35 minutes exercises (120 minutes total). For a shorter workshop, assign the independent challenge as homework.


    How Web Applications Work

    Delivery notes

    Use the four timing blocks above, with a break after request inspection. The challenge allocations include feedback. Keep the server running for both examples; restarting with the same database must preserve added records.

    Demonstrate developer tools slowly, enlarge their text, and name the selected request before switching panels. Accept the request transcripts as equivalent evidence for learners who cannot use developer tools. No SQL, framework setup, public hosting account, or authentication implementation is required.

    Watch for: the browser is the whole app; a success message proves saving; localStorage is shared; refreshing restarts the server; a database must run on a separate machine; a domain provides hosting; hiding a button authorises access.

    The final challenge is a design assessment. Keep deployment and full login implementation as extensions. During the daily reflection, ask learners to explain the journey from clicking Save to the displayed result in their own words. See the shared instructor notes.
